title: The $113M Sacrifice That Won New York A Ring: Will KAT Follow Brunson's Lead?
thumb_prompt: A weathered contract document torn in half with $113 million written in bold red ink, sitting next to an NBA championship trophy gleaming under dramatic spotlight in Madison Square Garden, the paper edges burning with orange and blue flames
thumb_subject: a determined point guard in a blue and orange number eleven jersey holding a championship trophy

paragraphs.text: Two months ago, the New York Knicks did something nobody thought possible. They won the championship. First time in fifty three years. Jalen Brunson scored forty five points in Game Five in San Antonio and brought the Larry O'Brien Trophy back to Manhattan. Finals MVP. Unanimous. Every single voter chose him. But here is the thing nobody wants to talk about today. The reason that championship exists, the reason Brunson had Karl-Anthony Towns next to him, the reason Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby were on that floor? It started with a sacrifice nobody saw coming. One hundred and thirteen million dollars. That is what Brunson left on the table in twenty twenty four when he signed his extension. He could have waited. Could have gotten the full supermax. Instead, he took one hundred fifty six point five million over four years and told the front office: build around me.

That decision changed everything. It gave Leon Rose the financial flexibility to trade for Mikal Bridges. Six first round picks, the biggest haul in franchise history, but the Knicks could only stomach that deal because Brunson was not eating up thirty percent of the cap. Then came Karl-Anthony Towns. Shipped Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo to Minnesota for the big man who would become the third best player on a championship team. None of it happens if Brunson gets greedy. None of it happens if he chooses himself over the team. And now, in August of twenty twenty six, the Knicks are asking the same question of Towns. Will you sacrifice too?

Here is the reality check hitting New York right now. Towns is eligible for a four year, two hundred seventy two million dollar extension. The full max. The biggest contract the Knicks can legally offer. And according to James Edwards at The Athletic, they are not going to give it to him. They will offer him an extension, yes. But not the max. Not even close. The Knicks are trying to stay under the second apron, and a full max deal for Towns would blow that up. Josh Hart might be gone. Miles McBride might be gone. The flexibility that won them the title would vanish overnight. So the question becomes: does Karl-Anthony Towns follow Jalen Brunson and take a discount? Or does he demand every penny he is owed?

Let me be clear about something. When we talk about players taking discounts, we are talking about generational wealth either way. Jalen Brunson did not become poor when he signed for one hundred fifty six million instead of two hundred seventy. Karl-Anthony Towns will not struggle if he takes two hundred twenty million instead of two hundred seventy two. These are enormous numbers. But in the NBA, ego matters. Pride matters. Your contract is your value. It is how the league measures you against your peers. When you take less, you are admitting you are not worth the max. You are saying: I am not that guy. Even if you won Finals MVP. Even if you delivered a championship. That is the mental battle.
card_lines: Taking less = admitting you're not max

paragraphs.text: And here is where it gets complicated for Towns. Jalen Brunson is a New York kid. Grew up in New Jersey. Father played in the league. He understands the Knicks, understands what winning here means. He took less because legacy mattered more than money. But Towns? He spent nine years in Minnesota being the guy. The franchise cornerstone. He is two years into his Knicks tenure. Won the chip, sure, but he was the third option behind Brunson and Mikal Bridges. Is that enough to make him sacrifice fifty million dollars? Is two years in New York enough to override nine years of being told you are a max player?

The other complication is Mitchell Robinson. The Knicks already lost him to the second apron monster. Robinson signed a three year, forty seven point three million dollar deal with the Celtics in July. The Knicks could have matched it, could have kept their backup center who grabbed the biggest offensive rebound of the Finals, but James Dolan drew a line. No second apron. Not negotiable. So they let Robinson walk and replaced him with Andre Drummond on a one year minimum deal. That is the cost of staying flexible. You lose beloved players. You lose guys who helped you win. And Towns sees that. He knows what the organization is willing to sacrifice.

Robinson spent eight years in New York. Drafted in twenty eighteen with the thirty sixth pick. Developed into one of the best rebounders in the league. He secured the offensive board off Josh Hart's missed free throw with twenty six seconds left in Game Five of the Finals, Knicks up three, season on the line. That rebound might have saved the championship. And two weeks later, he is packing his bags for Boston because the Knicks would not pay him sixteen million a year. If that is how they treat an eight year veteran who delivered in the biggest moment, what does that tell Towns about his own negotiation?
card_lines: Still let him walk weeks later

paragraphs.text: Let me take you back to two thousand ten. The Miami Heat are being built. LeBron James, Dwyane Wade, Chris Bosh. The Big Three. Everyone remembers the decision, the villain arc, the titles. But here is what people forget: all three of them took less than the max to make it work. They each left money on the table so Pat Riley could build a deeper roster around them. And it worked. Four straight Finals. Two championships. That is the blueprint. That is what the Knicks are trying to replicate. Brunson already played his part. Now they need Towns to do the same.

But there is a counter example too. The Dallas Mavericks in twenty eleven. Dirk Nowitzki took less money for years to help the Mavs build around him. And it worked. Championship. But after that? The front office whiffed on every major decision. Bad contracts. Bad trades. Dirk kept sacrificing, kept taking discounts, and Dallas could not build another contender around him. He never got back to the Finals. That is the risk for Towns. What if he takes two hundred twenty million instead of two seventy two, and the Knicks still cannot repeat? What if Leon Rose makes the wrong moves and the window closes? Then Towns gave up fifty million for nothing.

And then there is the Golden State model. Stephen Curry signed a team friendly extension in twenty twelve and twenty thirteen because of his ankle issues. That underpay allowed the Warriors to keep Klay Thompson, add Andre Iguodala, eventually sign Kevin Durant. Three championships in four years. Curry eventually got paid, got his supermax, but those early discounts built a dynasty. The Knicks are hoping Towns sees that. Hoping he understands that taking less now could mean three or four more rings down the line. But Curry was a Warriors lifer. He is still there today. Towns has been a Knick for two seasons. It is a different calculation.
card_lines: Built room for Klay, Iggy, KD

paragraphs.text: The other factor nobody talks about enough: what happens in two years? Towns is under contract for next season at fifty seven million, then he has a player option for sixty one million in twenty twenty seven to twenty eight. If he does not sign an extension now, he could opt out and hit free agency in twenty twenty eight. At that point, who knows what the cap looks like? Who knows what teams have space? He could get his full max then. Or the market could dry up and he is left with less than what the Knicks are offering today. That is the gamble. Sign now for security, or bet on yourself and wait.

Here is what makes this whole situation so fascinating. Jalen Brunson did not just take a discount. He set a standard. He created an expectation inside that locker room that winning matters more than money. Josh Hart took less. OG Anunoby took less. Mikal Bridges is on a team friendly deal. Everyone bought in. And now Towns is the test case. Is he part of that culture, or is he the outlier? Because if he demands the full max and the Knicks say no, what happens? Does he get traded? Does he play out his contract and leave? Does it create tension that destroys the chemistry that won the championship?

The Knicks fans are watching this too. Social media is already divided. Some people think Towns deserves every penny. He was incredible in the Finals. Averaged sixteen points and eleven rebounds against the Spurs. Hit huge shots. Played through injuries. He earned the max. But others say: you are the third option. You are not Jalen Brunson. You did not score forty five in the closeout game. You did not win Finals MVP. So why do you deserve the same money as the guys who did? It is brutal. It is unfair. But it is the reality of playing in New York. Your worth is debated on talk radio every single day.
card_lines: Fan base divided on KAT's value

paragraphs.text: The August eleventh deadline came and went. Towns did not sign an extension. Neither did Miles McBride, who has his own contract situation brewing. That tells you the Knicks and Towns are not on the same page yet. The front office is offering something south of the max. Towns wants more. The gap has not closed. And the longer this drags on, the more speculation builds. Trade rumors. Tension. All the things that can poison a locker room. The Knicks need to figure this out before training camp in October, or this story becomes the distraction that derails the repeat bid.

Let me give you my take. I think Towns signs. I think he takes something between two hundred and two hundred twenty million over four years. Not the full max, but enough to feel respected. Enough to tell himself he did not give away everything. And I think the Knicks find a way to make it work under the second apron. They will have to get creative. Maybe they trade a future pick to move salary. Maybe they convince Josh Hart to restructure. But they will figure it out. Because losing Towns after winning the championship would be an unmitigated disaster. It would signal to every future free agent that New York does not take care of its stars. That would haunt them for years.

Here is the thing about championships. They buy you credibility. They buy you leverage. Before June fourteenth, Karl-Anthony Towns was a talented big man who never made it past the second round. Great stats, empty resume. Now he is an NBA champion. Now he has a ring. That changes the negotiation. It means he can walk into Leon Rose's office and say: I helped deliver this. I was part of the solution. Pay me. But it also means the Knicks can say: we gave you this platform. We traded for you. We put you in position to win. Now help us win again. It is a two way street.

If Towns takes the discount and the Knicks win another championship, maybe two more, he becomes a New York legend. His number hangs in the rafters next to Ewing and Reed and Frazier. Kids grow up wearing his jersey. That is the upside. But if he demands the max and forces the Knicks to break up the core, and they never win again? He becomes the guy who chose money over legacy. He becomes the cautionary tale. The player who had it all and lost it because of greed. That is a heavy burden to carry in a city like New York. The back pages do not forget. The talk shows do not forgive.

Think about what Jalen Brunson already has. He is twenty nine years old. Finals MVP. NBA champion. Team captain. He gave the Knicks their first title in fifty three years. He scored forty five points in the biggest game in franchise history. No matter what happens the rest of his career, he is immortal in New York. Statues, banners, documentaries. All of it. And he got there by sacrificing one hundred thirteen million dollars. That is the model. That is what the Knicks are selling to Towns. Do you want to be rich, or do you want to be remembered? Because in New York, you can not always have both.

The other piece of this is Mikal Bridges. He came to New York in the summer of twenty twenty four. The Knicks gave up six first round picks for him. Massive haul. And Bridges said he never wanted to be traded that much, but now he is all in. He proved it in the Finals. Fourteen points in Game Five. Lockdown defense on Victor Wembanyama when it mattered. He is on a team friendly deal through twenty twenty nine. He already bought in. If Bridges took less and Towns demands more, what message does that send? It creates a hierarchy. It says: my value is greater than yours. That can fracture a team faster than anything else.

Look, this is the defining decision of the Knicks' offseason. Everything else is secondary. Replacing Mitchell Robinson with Andre Drummond, drafting Jack Kayil and Tyler Nickel, re-signing Jose Alvarado and Landry Shamet. All of that matters. But none of it matters as much as locking in Karl-Anthony Towns at a number that keeps this core together. Because if the Knicks lose Towns, or if they pay him so much that they have to gut the roster around him, the championship window slams shut. You do not win titles with two stars. You need depth. You need versatility. You need the kind of roster that can survive injuries and foul trouble and off nights. That is what Brunson's discount built. That is what they need Towns to preserve.

So here we are. August twelfth, twenty twenty six. Two months removed from the greatest moment in Knicks history. The parade is over. The rings are being sized. And the front office is sitting in a room with Karl-Anthony Towns and his agent, trying to find the number that keeps everyone happy. Trying to figure out if the culture Jalen Brunson built is strong enough to survive the negotiation. Trying to decide if one hundred thirteen million dollars of sacrifice is a one time anomaly or the new standard in New York. We will find out soon enough. Training camp is sixty days away. The clock is ticking. And the entire basketball world is watching to see if the Knicks can keep this thing together. Or if the second apron will tear it all apart.
